classification.difficultyReason: Development: students read paired columns, compare phone ownership relative to each cohort's size, justify the Year 9–10 likelihood comparison using percentages, and identify a proportional trend. The hardest demand links graph interpretation with the explicitly taught percentage procedure.

inlines.text: The graph below displays data collected at a school on the number of students
in each Year group, who own a mobile phone.

spec.sourceRegion: Question 13 grouped column graph and upper-right legend
spec.description: Adjacent paired columns with white total-student columns on the left and black stippled phone-owner columns on the right. The matched two-row legend remains outside the plot at upper right. Horizontal dotted gridlines occur every five students.
spec.answerVisibility: Both complete series and the legend are supplied givens. No calculated percentages or part answers appear.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Which Year group has the highest percentage of students with mobile phones?

answer.worked: Year 12: $\dfrac{50}{50}\times100\%=100\%$. All Year 12 students own a phone; every other Year group has fewer phone owners than students.

inlines.text: Two students are chosen at random, one from Year 9 and one from Year 10.
Which student is more likely to own a mobile phone?
Justify your answer with suitable calculations

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\text{Year 9 percentage} &= \frac{55}{70}\times100\%\\&\approx79\%\\\text{Year 10 percentage} &= \frac{50}{60}\times100\%\\&\approx83\%\end{align*}$$
The Year 10 student is more likely to own a mobile phone because the proportion is greater.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Identify a trend in the data shown in the graph.

answer.short: The proportion of students who own a mobile phone increases with Year group.
answer.worked: The proportion owning a phone increases with Year group, from $\dfrac{45}{75}=60\%$ in Year 7 to $\dfrac{50}{50}=100\%$ in Year 12.
